plan.title: 4 tips for your first time
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: Read the Crew Roles script word for word the first time. It's written to land.
Explain AI as "a friend who's never seen the picture." The clearer the words, the better the result.
If a pair gets stuck, suggest one change: add a color word, or say where things are.
Don't fix their prompts. The struggle is the lesson.

warmup.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Read the role scripts word for word the first time.
Call the AI "a friend who's never seen the picture."
If a pair is stuck, suggest adding a color word.

learn.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Share your own "Me" connection first, in under 30 seconds, to show the depth you want.
Point to the sentence starter when a girl gets stuck.
If you hear "she's a woman like me," ask what about her path stands out.

tryit.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: After each video pause, ask one question: "What did the video just say AI uses to learn?"
Let girls disagree on "Is it intelligent?" You don't need to settle it.
For MusicFX, offer one prompt shape: "[Genre] song with [instrument] in the style of [artist]."

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Give two quiet minutes to write before anyone talks.
Ask for volunteers on the last question. Don't call on anyone for it.

plan.title: 4 tips for this lesson
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: Expect high energy in MusicFX and a dip during Marmoset. Use the Hype Squad to bridge it.
Girls will want to skip the mind map. Don't let them: the mind map is the prompt engineering.
Show 2 or 3 Marmoset examples on the projector before girls explore.
Tracks that miss the genre are useful. They teach prompting.

warmup.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Accept any wording during the recall.
If a crew is stuck, give a starter: "AI learns by looking at lots of ___."
Keep a simple sheet of who has held each role.

learn.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Say: "Computers can't hear music, so people give them words to describe it."
Show 2 or 3 Marmoset searches before girls explore.
Think out loud while you build the prompt, mistakes included.

tryit.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Check mind maps at the 5-minute mark. If one is blank, fill it in together: "What instruments do you hear?"
For the Afrobeats map, offer starter words: drums, percussion, energetic, joyful, building. Girls add one of their own.
Mind map before MusicFX, every round.

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Write KEEP / TRY / CHANGE on the board.
If a girl is stuck, offer: "Keep the drums. Try a faster tempo. Change the mood word from chill to energetic."

plan.title: 4 tips for this lesson
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: Build a sample model yourself before class. It takes 10 minutes.
Webcams fail? Switch to the Image Project and train on photos.
Push crews for variety: one dancer in one outfit means the model only knows her.
Watch for crews training on faces instead of poses.

warmup.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Stuck crews: "AI is great at dogs because there are millions of dog photos online. It's bad at left-handed scissors because nobody photographs them."
Don't explain bias yet. Let the examples sit.

learn.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Say "examples" instead of "samples" and "groups" instead of "classes."
Explain the percentage: "The AI is guessing, and it tells you how sure it is."
Walk through every button on screen.

tryit.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: At 10 minutes, check sample counts. Under 20 per move? Add 10 more with a different dancer.
Catch crews training on faces instead of poses.
When the model guesses wrong, ask: "What does the AI think this is? Why?"

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Stay with their own example: "If your AI only saw one person dancing, it wouldn't recognize anyone else."
Then connect it: the same thing happens when face recognition is trained on one kind of face.

plan.title: 4 tips for this lesson
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: Your energy sets the tone. This is a celebration, not a test.
Announce each crew yourself and lead the clap-in.
Keep transitions between crews under 30 seconds.
Celebrate every crew equally, mistakes included.

warmup.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Let each crew pick its own performance length.
Keep the brief on the board all lesson.

learn.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Offer 3 shapes: everyone in unison; a solo, then the crew joins one by one; or two pairs doing call-and-response.
Coach in four steps: pick moves, practice slowly, add the music, practice the order.

tryit.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Announce each crew and lead the clap-in.
If a Speaker freezes on the AI part, prompt: "Tell us one prompt word your crew used."
If she freezes on the intro: "Tell us your crew name."

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Put sentence starters on the board for the reflection form.
Keep it celebratory. Every girl stands for her role.

plan.title: 4 tips for your first time
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: Expect high energy at the start, a dip during the algorithm math, then a lift at Canva. Use the Hype Squad to bridge the dip.
Make the math concrete: "100 likes but 50 angry emojis. Which algorithm pushes it harder?"
Girls who skip social media have a valuable outside view. Say so.
Canva can swallow time. Hold the 20-minute limit.

warmup.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Tell girls what to listen for before you press play.
Let girls name content they love, then steer the talk to patterns, not posts.
If a girl doesn't post, ask why her friends share what they share.

learn.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Walk one case study out loud first: what happened, why share it, how it feels, where the surprise is.
If the Algorithm 2 idea doesn't land, try this: "50 angry comments, or 50 quiet likes. Which post wins?"
Ask for real examples of a feed narrowing or widening someone's view.

tryit.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Suggest a layout: title, three points, one picture per point, one closing line.
Ask for one specific fact. "Algorithms can be harmful" isn't enough. How?

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Keep each round to 4 minutes with a timer.
Hand out sticky notes before the walk starts, not during.

plan.title: 4 tips for this lesson
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: Energy runs very high during dancing and lower during the TikTok video. Use the Hype Squad to bridge.
Give credit: Reggaeton comes from Puerto Rico and Panama. Don't let the moves lose their roots.
Always offer the gentler version of el perreo first, and use consent language.
Point "I want to be famous" talk back to the project question.

warmup.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Dance with them. Don't perform: take part.
You don't need to be good. Your job is to show the room is safe to dance in.

learn.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Sum up the rest of the TikTok video in your own words. Three sentences is plenty.
Try framing it both ways: computers help us find new music, and computers might choose for us.
Beat out the dembow on a table: boom, ch, boom, chick.

tryit.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Trust the tutorial videos. Keep crews on them and encourage.
Validate the gentler versions out loud.
Use dance words if you know them: isolation, weight transfer, hip hinge.

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Offer three ways to open a video: a question, a surprising fact or a striking picture.
Push for one concrete change, not a general wish.

plan.title: 4 tips for this lesson
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: This is the newest lesson. Walk through the card sort and Teachable Machine yourself first, even if you've taught before.
Let girls set likes to 10. Then let the feed show them what happens.
Some girls will ask why this matters. Connect it to their own feed: what if it's making you anxious or angry?
Stay open to disagreement. There's no single right answer here.

warmup.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Ask: "You said you want less news. Have you tried to change that?"
Girls without social media can describe a friend's feed.

learn.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Work one example on the board: 100 likes at weight 1 plus 50 comments at weight 5 scores 350.
Say it plainly: platforms chose these weights.

tryit.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Have crews agree on the goal before anyone sets a weight.
Walk one crew through the classifier, then let other crews copy.
Ask: "Could someone else label this post differently?"

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Use the recipe again: taste, health or speed. Which cake would you bake?
Write the "2 changes" answers where everyone can see them.

plan.title: 4 tips for this lesson
plan.sub: For volunteers and first-time facilitators. STEM teachers can skip ahead.
tips: Your energy sets the tone. This is a celebration, not a test.
Draw names for the showcase order.
Have a backup: if filming fails, crews perform live.
This lesson works best in one block. If you must split it, break after filming.

warmup.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Keep roles the same all lesson so crews can focus.
Write the brief on the board so crews can check it while they film.

learn.title: 3 tips for this step
tips: Offer three openings: a surprising statement, one striking move, or a question.
Step in only if a video will miss the brief. Ask, "Where does the audience hear your message?"
Push for one full take early, then reshoot.

tryit.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Hype each crew briefly before its premiere.
Let girls answer audience questions before you do.

reflect.title: 2 tips for this step
tips: Give three quiet minutes to write before anyone shares.
Name what each girl did when you hand out her sticker.
